title: When Your Kids Fight, Are You a Witness or a Judge?
dek: The biggest mistake parents make when stepping into sibling conflict is refereeing with their own childhood fairness wounds. What kids need isn't a verdict on who was right, but practice repairing the relationship inside low-stakes conflict.
why: Medium information density with a clear core framework: witness not judge, sportscaster mode, fairness is not equality. Best for parents with more than one child, especially those whose own childhood emotions get triggered by sibling fights.
who: Parents with more than one child, especially those whose childhood fairness wounds get triggered by sibling fights and who tend to rush in and referee.

points.h: Deal with your own sibling baggage before you step in
points.body: The episode opens by pointing out that almost everyone carries sibling baggage — even without siblings, there's either a longing for that ‘mythical connection’ or relief at not having it. The fairness trap is the thing most likely to trigger a parent's emotions: a cake sliced unevenly, a rule that was looser for one kid, a new dress given to only one of them — those memories get activated the moment you see your own kids fighting. If you step in before dealing with that baggage, you're effectively imposing your sibling history on your children. So the first step is always clearing your own head, not rushing in to hand down a verdict.

points.h: You are a witness, not a judge
points.body: This is the single most important line in the whole piece, and Dr. Pressman repeats it more than a dozen times. When you start deciding who's right, who hit first, who was worse, that judgment comes from your own history, not from what actually happened between these two kids right now. As a witness, your job is to observe and describe, not to rule. That distinction determines your tone, your words, and your posture when you step in. Once you become the judge, you'll unconsciously favor, convict, and punish — and what the kids feel isn't justice, it's your unfinished childhood emotions making decisions for them.

Dr. Pressman gives clear signals for stepping in: a child is in danger, there's a power imbalance, or they're stuck in a loop they can't get out of. If the two are evenly matched and physically safe, you can stay nearby and occasionally ask ‘Is everyone okay?’ But watch especially for power dynamics turning into toxic bullying — rare, but when it happens, an adult must cut it off. Kids who've experienced peer or sibling bullying have much worse adult outcomes, and the damage is far greater than we realize. Bullying has a strict definition, though: a power difference plus repeated, malicious, intentional abuse. Just ‘being a jerk’ isn't bullying, and kids being jerks to each other is completely normal.

If you do need to step in, Dr. Pressman recommends ‘sportscaster mode’ — you act like an observant, reflective commentator who just describes what happened. For example, ‘I noticed this happened over here, and that happened over there — did I get that right?’ This lets you validate both kids at once, without taking sides, without a winner. The key is avoiding questions like ‘Who started it?’ ‘You always do this,’ ‘There's something wrong with you.’ When you tell a child there's something wrong with who they are rather than with a behavior, you're feeding the exact habit you don't want them using on each other — turning anger and outbursts into a question about a person's worth. ‘You're stupid’ means ‘You are a stupid person,’ and no one needs to hear that.

points.h: Stop dehumanizing language on the spot
points.body: Dr. Pressman says kids can scream, yell, be vicious to each other, even get physical — but if she hears dehumanizing language, she'll pause the fight right there to change the wording. Because what you want to constantly ‘wire’ and ‘bake’ into your kids is: talk about the behavior, not about who the person is. This isn't a lesson afterward, it's immediate intervention. She'll say in that moment, ‘Let's say that a different way.’ The logic behind it: language habits need repeated reinforcement to internalize, and every dehumanizing expression that gets let slide is reinforcement in the wrong direction.

Dr. Pressman uses the peanut butter cupcake example to explain the difference between fair and equal: giving two kids identical peanut butter cupcakes, same size, same recipe, looks equal — but if one of them is allergic to peanuts, it's completely unfair. Fair means giving each child what they need, not giving everyone the same thing. This framework protects you when a kid demands ‘Why does my 12-year-old sister get a phone and I don't?’ — you can answer, ‘You're different people, I've learned more since then, and I'm making a different decision that's better for you.’ If you try to be perfectly equal, you're assuming every child is the same age, same personality, same temperament, same interests, same needs — which obviously doesn't hold.

Dr. Pressman points out that giving all your kids the same label (like ‘you're all helpers’) can indeed promote positive behavior, but labeling only one child in the family as ‘the helper’ creates tension and problematic dynamics. Labels plant seeds of resentment, insecurity, and lack of motivation, and they push siblings apart. Teachers, friends, other parents, relatives — they all label. A parent's job is to counteract that damage, not join in. Labels ‘haunt’ a child — Dr. Pressman uses the word haunt, and says it sounds dramatic but it's true.

Dr. Pressman distinguishes real repair from fake repair. Repair isn't necessarily a public apology — if the kids finish fighting and suddenly start giggling together, sharing an inside joke, making faces at each other, that's repair, that's reconnection, and you're witnessing it. Every reconnection strengthens the relationship, teaching kids ‘this relationship is forever, it gets messy, but we always come back.’ But a forced apology isn't repair. Saying ‘sorry’ and saying ‘apologize to your brother’ don't teach what the research literature calls repair. An insincere apology just makes people angrier. You can ask, ‘How do you think that made your sibling feel? Is there anything you could do to help them feel better?’ If the child says no, you don't just drop it — you come back later and ask, ‘Have you had time to think about that?’

points.h: Be curious, not punitive, with the instigator
points.body: When one child repeatedly instigates, Dr. Pressman suggests first telling the other child, ‘I've noticed your sister started it the last few times, and I also see how hard you're trying to avoid a fight. I know this is hard, and we'll keep practicing these skills.’ With the instigator, start with genuine curiosity: why are they instigating so often? Do they need more one-on-one time? Is there something you haven't noticed that they're longing for, jealous of, or needing? Then find a way to meet that need without depriving the other child. If you just yell ‘It's always you starting things’ and punish, you haven't taught them the underlying skill or self-reflection — ‘Why do I keep starting this? What do I actually want?’ Teaching the instigator to figure out what they want and find a productive way to get it is one of the most important skills.

points.h: Forced family time is an underrated ritual
points.body: Dr. Pressman says one of her favorite currently unpopular things is ‘forced family time.’ She often hears parents say, ‘We used to have dinner together on Friday nights, but then the kids didn't want to come, they had other things to do or friends to see.’ She believes finding one sacred, non-negotiable family time each week matters. Maybe kids can invite friends, but you can't give up the time. We tend to fear kids will be annoyed at being forced to spend time together, but forced family time isn't about doing it every time — it's about certain things being sacred to the family that cultivate and build connection. Even if both kids are annoyed by the tradition, it's something they can complain about together, a time of connection, and once it becomes ‘just the way it is,’ it stops being a fight.

points.h: Kids uniting against you is healthy
points.body: Dr. Pressman shares a story from the car: her two daughters were fighting in the back seat, she got very annoyed, said something in a tone that maybe got a little out of control, and they started laughing at how out of control she was, stopped fighting, and even started helping her regulate her emotions. Annoying in the moment, but she was thrilled to see them discover ‘when they unite against me, they're a team.’ She specifically notes that if one child is difficult and the other child allies with you to complain about the difficult sibling, she's less interested in that dynamic — she's more interested in them uniting against you. That's much healthier, and it's the picture you want to see long-term.

Dr. Pressman encourages mixed-age play. There's a trend now of five-year-olds playing with five-year-olds and seven-year-olds with seven-year-olds, but really you should mix ages together, like the old-fashioned neighborhood where whoever was around played in the cul-de-sac. Kids of different ages can be both teacher and learner, both big contributor and little kid still learning. Also, every child should have their own dedicated playtime, but they should also find at least one shared interest — like the whole family playing wiffle ball, going to a play, picking a comedy to watch together. That shared interest should be separate from the individual hobbies the kids develop.

points.h: Make your kids cooperate to persuade you
points.body: Dr. Pressman suggests creating things that require your kids to cooperate, like if they want to go out to eat, they have to work together to persuade you to take them to their favorite restaurant. That way they don't have time to argue about which restaurant, because they're busy figuring out how to pitch the idea to Mom or Dad. You can also create fun little rituals that seem ‘anti-parent,’ like one day a week dessert before dinner, Wacky Wednesday, Silly Sunday, and have the kids come up with ideas together to persuade you. Anything that gets them cooperating works. Also, when you're at the grocery store with one child, ask what they think their sibling would like, getting them into each other's heads — that's the beginning of practicing larger interpersonal relationships, peer relationships, romantic relationships.

Dr. Pressman says calling siblings friends helps them treat each other like friends. The expectation is that from early on, they truly treat siblings like a deep friendship. There must be one non-negotiable rule in your family: your friends are not allowed to be mean to your sibling. That's when you teach siblings to have each other's backs. In this world, it's hard to feel like no one has your back, and knowing that at school, on the playground, out there, someone has your back — and that person is your sibling — is incredibly empowering, gives you a sense of belonging in being loved, and that belonging is very rare right now. So nip it early: no ganging up on a sibling, no friends being mean to a sibling.

points.h: The goal isn't no fighting — it's learning repair
points.body: Dr. Pressman says at the end that the sibling relationship is the longest relationship of your life. The goal isn't no fighting — let that dream die. The goal is learning to repair in a healthy, sincere way. Ask yourself: how do you want them to describe each other as adults? How do you want them to see each other as adults? Do you picture them laughing together? Build it now with deep understanding: along the way there will be some ugly fights, and that's part of the process.
